lessons.subject: mathematics
lessons.lesson_title: Height comes from one vertical side
lessons.previous_learning: Friday: 75%. Plotting and triangle halving improved. Height was incorrectly written as zero.
lessons.course_context: Day 29 builds from reviewed Day 28 work. Explain first; demonstrate; practice; check. Preserve original grades.
learning_objectives: Choose the correct two corners for height.
Find rectangle and right-triangle areas with units.
lessons.why_it_matters: Choose the correct two corners for height.

vocabulary.definition: A point address: (across, up), also called (x, y).
The up-and-down distance, not the point address.
A square 1 unit wide and 1 unit tall.

lessons.written_instruction:
TIME CAP: 50 minutes. 9:30-10:20. Stop at the end of this block.
9:30-9:35 START HERE. On Friday, you plotted the rectangle correctly. The next step is choosing the correct side to measure. A shape with visible height cannot have height zero.
9:35-9:45 LEARN. In (7,1), 7 is the across address and 1 is the up address. For height, pick two corners on ONE vertical side. Their across addresses match. Their up addresses change. Count the gaps, not the grid lines.
Look at B(7,1) and C(7,5) in the picture. Both are on x = 7. Move upward from y = 1 to y = 5: four gaps. Subtract the up addresses: 5 - 1 = 4 units. Using the two bottom corners would measure no upward change, not the rectangle height.
9:45-10:08 PRACTICE. Use the grid for M1. Label both points used for height before subtracting. Rectangle area is width times height. For a right triangle, multiply base by height that meets it at a square corner, then divide by 2. Perpendicular means the two directions make a square corner.
10:08-10:15 CHECK. Cover the model and try the exit. 10:15-10:20: correct one step with help or explain your method. Stop at 10:20.

worked_examples.title: Rectangle model
worked_examples.problem: A(2,1), B(7,1), C(7,5), D(2,5). Find height and area.
worked_examples.solution: B to C: 5 - 1 = 4. Width: 7 - 2 = 5. Area: 5 × 4 = 20 square units.
worked_examples.explanation: The two height points have the same x address. Count four gaps to check.

worked_examples.title: Triangle refresher
worked_examples.problem: A right triangle has base 8 units and height 3 units.
worked_examples.explanation: Two matching right triangles make the 8-by-3 rectangle.

independent_practice.prompt: M1. Plot A(1,2), B(6,2), C(6,6), D(1,6). Join the corners. Circle the two points you use for height. Show width, height and area.
independent_practice.answer: B,C or A,D; width 5, height 4, area 20 square units.

independent_practice.prompt: M2. A student compares (2,3) with (8,3) and says a rectangle has height 0. Its top corners are (2,7) and (8,7). Explain the mistake and find the actual height.
independent_practice.answer: Compared bottom corners; use same-x pair, 7 - 3 = 4 units.

independent_practice.prompt: M3. A right triangle has base 6 units and height 5 units. Show two calculations for its area.

exit_ticket.prompt: ME1. Rectangle corners: (3,1), (8,1), (8,4), (3,4). Name your height corners. Find width, height and area.
exit_ticket.answer: Same-x endpoints; width 5, height 3, area 15 square units.

exit_ticket.prompt: ME2. Find a right triangle area with base 7 and height 4 units. Show the halving step.

lessons.voice_prompt: Day 29 Monday October 5. Block 9:30-10:20; whole day 9:30 AM to 3:30 PM. Friday: 75%. Plotting and triangle halving improved. Height was incorrectly written as zero. Teach with the lesson picture and plain definitions before practice. Give one step, then wait. Use different examples, not assigned answers. Score M1 4, M2 2, M3 2, exits 2 each = 12. Both exit methods must be correct before combined area. Preserve September 30 missing-work status; these are new attempts. Parent update: use everyday words, explain one step at a time, and name the exact action to take. Keep the work challenging but make the directions easy to understand.
lessons.teacher_notes:
Score M1 4, M2 2, M3 2, exits 2 each = 12. Both exit methods must be correct before combined area. Preserve September 30 missing-work status; these are new attempts.
VISUAL GUIDE: The revised teaching pictures show twenty individual square tiles, fully numbered axes, four marked height gaps, and two matching triangles that fit an 8-by-3 rectangle. Refer to the exact tile or gap instead of just repeating the formula.

lessons.subject: writing
lessons.previous_learning: Friday: 85%. Exact evidence was good; one reason repeated the claim. Keep the short sentence-card approach.
lessons.course_context: Day 29 builds from reviewed Day 28 work. Explain first; demonstrate; practice; check. Preserve original grades.
learning_objectives: Connect a result to an idea using a real explanation.
Improve a sentence from your own paragraph.
lessons.why_it_matters: Connect a result to an idea using a real explanation.

vocabulary.definition: The idea you are trying to support.
A specific fact or result you can point to.
Your explanation of why that fact supports your idea.

lessons.written_instruction:
TIME CAP: 50 minutes. 10:30-11:20. Stop at the end of this block.
10:30-10:40 LEARN. Evidence answers: What happened? Reasoning answers: Why does that make my idea more likely? Saying the same idea twice is not an explanation.
MODEL: The lamp stays dark with Bulb A, lights with Bulb B, then stays dark with A again. A useful reason is: The lamp works with B, so Bulb A may be the problem because the lamp works with Bulb B.
10:40-10:50 ROBOT TEST RESULTS. These are invented test results for the same toy robot on the same route. Both batteries began fully charged. With Battery A it stopped after 8 minutes and its battery power reading dropped a lot. With Battery B it ran for 30 minutes without stopping. The battery was the only planned change. The tests suggest a problem with A, but do not prove every other part is perfect.
10:50-11:08 BUILD FOUR SENTENCES. 1: My idea is ___. 2: In the test, ___. 3: This supports my idea because ___. 4: To check further, I would ___. Say each sentence before writing. Include the 8-minute and 30-minute comparison; you may combine those facts into one sentence.
11:08-11:15 MAKE IT CLEARER. Choose one sentence you actually wrote. Copy it, improve it, and say why the new version is clearer. 11:15-11:20 EXIT. No long essay today.

worked_examples.title: Fact versus reason
worked_examples.problem: Lamp A/B test: which part is reasoning?
worked_examples.solution: Fact: B lit the lamp. Reason: This shows the lamp can work, so A is a more likely source of the problem.
worked_examples.explanation: The reason connects the result to the claim.

worked_examples.title: Make a reason clearer
worked_examples.problem: Original: The bulb is bad because it is broken.
worked_examples.solution: Improved: Bulb A may be faulty because the same lamp lights with B but not with A.
worked_examples.explanation: The improved sentence gives a comparison instead of repeating bad/broken.

independent_practice.prompt: W1. In the robot source, underline or copy two exact results that help compare A and B.
independent_practice.answer: A stopped at 8 minutes with sharp voltage drop; B ran 30 minutes without stopping.

independent_practice.prompt: W2. Use the four sentence frames to write one short paragraph. Give a reason, not just a repeated claim.
independent_practice.answer: A may be failing; exact 8/30 comparison; robot can run with B so issue follows A; repeat under same conditions or test another fully charged battery.

independent_practice.prompt: W3. Copy one sentence from W2. Write an improved version. Say what you made clearer.
independent_practice.answer: Actual original sentence, meaningful revision, explanation of improvement.

exit_ticket.prompt: WE1. Say or write: What does the successful Battery B test tell us about the robot? Why is may be failing more careful than definitely broken?
exit_ticket.answer: Robot can run under B condition; tests support A problem but do not rule out all other causes.

lessons.voice_prompt: Day 29 Monday October 5. Block 10:30-11:20; whole day 9:30 AM to 3:30 PM. Friday: 85%. Exact evidence was good; one reason repeated the claim. Keep the short sentence-card approach. Teach with the lesson picture and plain definitions before practice. Give one step, then wait. Use different examples, not assigned answers. Score evidence 4, paragraph claim 2/reason 4/further check 2, revision 4, exit 4 = 20. Accept short sentences and oral planning. Mark explanation quality, not length. Do not dictate assigned reasoning. Parent update: use everyday words, explain one step at a time, and name the exact action to take. Keep the work challenging but make the directions easy to understand.
lessons.teacher_notes:
Score evidence 4, paragraph claim 2/reason 4/further check 2, revision 4, exit 4 = 20. Accept short sentences and oral planning. Mark explanation quality, not length. Do not dictate assigned reasoning.
VISUAL GUIDE: The revised picture shows a recognizable navy desk lamp, unlit with A and lit with B, with the same desk and setup. Use the written A/B/A sequence. It is an illustrated hypothetical test, not a photo proving that an experiment occurred.

lessons.subject: french
lessons.lesson_title: Ask about plans; answer as yourself
lessons.previous_learning: Friday: 100%, including parent-observed oral checks. Introduce je vais rather than repeating only tu/nous.
lessons.course_context: Day 29 builds from reviewed Day 28 work. Explain first; demonstrate; practice; check. Preserve original grades.
learning_objectives: Ask a tu question and answer with je.
lessons.why_it_matters: Ask a tu question and answer with je.

vocabulary.definition: I
The form of aller used with je.
Tomorrow
To draw

lessons.written_instruction:
TIME CAP: 25 minutes. 11:20-11:45. Stop at the end of this block.
11:20-11:25 REVIEW. Tu vas lire means You are going to read. Nous allons lire means We are going to read. Today add Je vais lire: I am going to read.
11:25-11:32 LEARN. Build it: je + vais + action. The action stays in its basic form: lire, jouer, dessiner, regarder. To ask someone: Est-ce que tu vas lire ? To answer as yourself: Oui, je vais lire.
To say no: Non, je ne vais pas lire. Put ne before vais and pas after vais. The action stays after pas. Demain can go at the start: Demain, je vais dessiner.
11:32-11:40 WRITE F1-F3, then practise a short conversation with your parent. 11:40-11:45: your parent listens to three spoken sentences and marks correct or try again.

worked_examples.title: A question and reply
worked_examples.problem: Ask: Are you going to draw? Answer yes as yourself.
worked_examples.solution: Est-ce que tu vas dessiner ? Oui, je vais dessiner.
worked_examples.explanation: The question uses tu vas; your answer uses je vais.

worked_examples.title: A negative reply
worked_examples.problem: Say: I am not going to watch.
worked_examples.explanation: Ne and pas surround vais, not the action word.

independent_practice.prompt: F1. Translate: Tomorrow, I am going to play.
F2. Ask: Are you going to read? Then write a yes answer as yourself.
independent_practice.answer: Est-ce que tu vas lire ? Oui, je vais lire.

independent_practice.prompt: F3. Translate: I am not going to draw.

exit_ticket.prompt: FE1. Without looking at the example, say: I am going to read; Are you going to play?; I am not going to watch. Parent records correct or retry for each.
exit_ticket.answer: Je vais lire. Est-ce que tu vas jouer ? Je ne vais pas regarder.

lessons.voice_prompt: Day 29 Monday October 5. Block 11:20-11:45; whole day 9:30 AM to 3:30 PM. Friday: 100%, including parent-observed oral checks. Introduce je vais rather than repeating only tu/nous. Teach with the lesson picture and plain definitions before practice. Give one step, then wait. Use different examples, not assigned answers. Written 4 points (F2 two), oral 3 = 7. Observed oral only; do not infer speech from writing. Record observer and date. Correct je/tu switches gently. Parent update: use everyday words, explain one step at a time, and name the exact action to take. Keep the work challenging but make the directions easy to understand.
lessons.teacher_notes:
Written 4 points (F2 two), oral 3 = 7. Observed oral only; do not infer speech from writing. Record observer and date. Correct je/tu switches gently.
VISUAL GUIDE: The revised picture shows a girl asking a boy at an art table. The boy answers as himself. Point out tu vas in her question and je vais in his reply. These are illustrative classmates, not Atticus or named real people.

lessons.subject: science
lessons.lesson_title: Turn the mirror; check the light
lessons.previous_learning: Friday: 80%. Old route repaired, but first mirror in the new upward route tilted the wrong way.
lessons.course_context: Day 29 builds from reviewed Day 28 work. Explain first; demonstrate; practice; check. Preserve original grades.
learning_objectives: Choose a mirror tilt that matches the outgoing ray.
Draw and label a normal and equal reflection angles.
lessons.why_it_matters: Choose a mirror tilt that matches the outgoing ray.

vocabulary.definition: An arrow showing the direction light travels.
An imaginary guide line at a square corner to the mirror.
Light bouncing from a surface.
The place the ray meets the mirror.

lessons.written_instruction:
TIME CAP: 35 minutes. 11:45-12:20. Stop at the end of this block.
11:45-11:53 LEARN. Look at the two pictures. The same upward ray turns right from an up-right mirror, but left from a down-right mirror. Drawing the arrow you want does not make the mirror send light that way.
The normal is not another mirror. It is a dashed measuring guide at 90 degrees to the mirror. When the mirror turns, the normal turns too. Measure the coming-in and going-out angles from the normal, on opposite sides. These two angles match.
11:53-12:08 DRAW. Use a ruler. For a 90-degree turn, a 45-degree diagonal mirror sits between the coming-in and going-out directions. Draw the mirror first, its normal next, and the arrows last. Label hit point, mirror and normal. Mark a small square between mirror and normal.
12:08-12:15 explain and check. 12:15-12:20 correct one tilt or label. No laser is needed; this is a paper light-path model.

worked_examples.title: One upward ray
worked_examples.problem: Which tilt sends an upward ray to the right?
worked_examples.solution: An up-right mirror. Its normal tilts down-right. The ray angles from that normal are 45 degrees each.
worked_examples.explanation: The dashed guide is perpendicular to the solid mirror.

worked_examples.title: Angles from the guide
worked_examples.problem: The incoming angle is 35 degrees from the normal.
worked_examples.solution: The outgoing angle is 35 degrees, on the other side of the normal.
worked_examples.explanation: Do not measure from the mirror surface instead.

independent_practice.prompt: S1. Draw an UP then RIGHT then UP route with two mirrors. Choose both tilts. Label both normals and hit points, show arrowheads, and mark both right-angle squares. Mark each equal angle pair.
independent_practice.answer: Both mirrors tilt up-right; normals down-right; two genuine turns with paired 45-degree angles.

independent_practice.prompt: S2. In one or two sentences, explain why changing Mirror 1 can make the ray miss Mirror 2. Mention the normal.
independent_practice.answer: Mirror and normal rotate; reflected direction changes and can miss second mirror.

exit_ticket.prompt: SE1. Without the picture: an upward ray must leave to the LEFT. Sketch the mirror and normal. Then answer: if an incoming angle is 25 degrees from the normal, what is the outgoing angle?
exit_ticket.answer: Mirror down-right, normal up-right; outgoing 25 degrees from normal.

lessons.voice_prompt: Day 29 Monday October 5. Block 11:45-12:20; whole day 9:30 AM to 3:30 PM. Friday: 80%. Old route repaired, but first mirror in the new upward route tilted the wrong way. Teach with the lesson picture and plain definitions before practice. Give one step, then wait. Use different examples, not assigned answers. Score S1 tilts 4/normals and right angles 4/arrows and hit points 2/equal angles 2; S2 4; exit 4 = 20. Judge intended geometry, not camera perspective or perfect freehand measurement. Hold new optics if transfer tilt remains wrong. Parent update: use everyday words, explain one step at a time, and name the exact action to take. Keep the work challenging but make the directions easy to understand.
lessons.teacher_notes: Score S1 tilts 4/normals and right angles 4/arrows and hit points 2/equal angles 2; S2 4; exit 4 = 20. Judge intended geometry, not camera perspective or perfect freehand measurement. Hold new optics if transfer tilt remains wrong.

lessons.subject: history_geography
lessons.previous_learning: Friday: 100%. Geography plus human action is understood. Move to a first look at republican government.
lessons.course_context: Day 29 builds from reviewed Day 28 work. Explain first; demonstrate; practice; check. Preserve original grades.
learning_objectives: Explain why sharing power did not give everyone an equal voice.

vocabulary.definition: A government without a king, with public offices and a role for citizens.
One of Rome’s two leading elected officials.
An influential council that advised officials.
A group of citizens meeting to vote.

lessons.written_instruction:
TIME CAP: 35 minutes. 1:00-1:35. Stop at the end of this block.
1:00-1:05 CONNECT. The river and farmland helped Rome, but people had to use them. Rules and government are human choices, not parts of the land.
1:05-1:12 VIDEO. With a parent, open Khan Academy: Roman social and political structures. Watch up to 5 minutes, pausing once to name a group you hear. Do not try to memorise every term. If playback fails, use the picture and reading below; the lesson is complete without the video.
VIDEO LINK: https://www.khanacademy.org/humanities/world-history/ancient-medieval/roman-empire/v/roman-social-and-political-structures
1:12-1:20 READ. According to Roman tradition, the Republic began in 509 BCE (more than 2,500 years ago). Rome had elected officials rather than a king. Two consuls shared leading duties, usually for one year. The Senate was a group of powerful people who gave advice and helped shape decisions. Assemblies were groups of male citizens who voted for leaders or on laws. This is a simple map of roles, not a modern three-branch government.
A republic did not mean everyone had an equal voice. Women and enslaved people could not vote. Rich people and families with high standing often had more power. Ordinary citizens worked over many years to gain more say in government. Roman government changed across centuries.
1:20-1:30 use the picture for H1-H2. 1:30-1:35 finish the exit. Laws are human-made rules; writing a law does not guarantee everyone obeys it.

worked_examples.title: An imaginary club
worked_examples.problem: A club has two leaders serving one month. How could this limit one person’s power?
worked_examples.solution: They share responsibility, and the term ends.
worked_examples.explanation: This models sharing power; it is not a claim that a club is identical to Rome.

worked_examples.title: An unequal vote
worked_examples.problem: An imaginary club lets only some members vote. Is everyone equally represented?
worked_examples.solution: No. People excluded from voting have less say.
worked_examples.explanation: A voting system can exist without equal participation.

independent_practice.prompt: H1. Match each job to consuls, Senate or assemblies: leading elected officials; influential advisers; groups that vote.
H2. Explain one way Rome shared political power, and name one group excluded from voting.
independent_practice.answer: Two consuls or assemblies/Senate roles; women or enslaved people.

exit_ticket.prompt: HE1. Correct this claim in two short sentences: Rome was a republic, so every person had an equal say.
exit_ticket.answer: Government had citizen participation but voting excluded women and enslaved people; power also unequal among citizens.

lessons.voice_prompt: Day 29 Monday October 5. Block 1:00-1:35; whole day 9:30 AM to 3:30 PM. Friday: 100%. Geography plus human action is understood. Move to a first look at republican government. Teach with the lesson picture and plain definitions before practice. Give one step, then wait. Use different examples, not assigned answers. H1 3, H2 4, exit 3 = 10. No test of untaught video details. Teacher background source OpenStax contains mature founding narratives; do not assign the full background page to the student. Roles lesson only. Parent update: use everyday words, explain one step at a time, and name the exact action to take. Keep the work challenging but make the directions easy to understand.
lessons.teacher_notes:
H1 3, H2 4, exit 3 = 10. No test of untaught video details. Teacher background source OpenStax contains mature founding narratives; do not assign the full background page to the student. Roles lesson only.
VISUAL GUIDE: The revised picture shows people in three distinct roles: two consuls, senators debating, and male citizens in an outdoor assembly. These are artistic reconstructions, not portraits of named people or exact buildings. Explain the captions and excluded voters; do not infer historical facts from incidental architectural details.

lessons.subject: computer_science
lessons.unit_title: Create a 3D vehicle and reveal trailer
lessons.lesson_title: HOVER ONE: build a 3D hover-car in Blender
lessons.previous_learning: Museum After Dark earned 90%. Reset debugging and creative direction are credited. Parent requests broader ambitious projects, not automatic small game edits.
lessons.course_context: One assigned multi-session project. Today build seven editable 3D parts, use AI coaching, render a poster and save/reopen. Supersedes Sky Run and all earlier Day 29 project menus.
learning_objectives: Build and colour an original seven-part hover-car in Blender.
Use one clear AI request, then judge the suggested change by looking at the result.
Save an editable .blend file and a .png poster, and reopen both.
lessons.why_it_matters: Game vehicles start as models made by artists. Today you make your own vehicle and its first reveal image, inspired by Rocket League. Next session, this same car will move.

vocabulary.definition: A 3D object you can turn around.
The paint and surface finish of a part.
Make a copy.
Make the finished picture using the camera and lights.
Trim a sharp edge.

lessons.written_instruction:
TIME CAP: 60 minutes. 1:35-2:35. Parent setup happens beforehand.
Your project: HOVER ONE — 1:35-1:40 · Open and save
Build an original hover-car in Blender. Make a poster image of it today. Next time, we will make this same car move. Rocket League is the connection: artists create a vehicle model before it can appear in a game. This is your own design, not a Rocket League mod.
Open Blender 5.2. Close its welcome picture by clicking outside it. Choose File > Open. Find the parent-checked Hover-Studio.blend in Downloads, select it, and click Open Blender File. If asked, do not enable Python scripts; this scene needs none.
You should see an empty round stage. The camera, lights and paint colours are ready. There is no car in the starting file. If your view is not inside a camera frame, use View > Cameras > Active Camera from the menu above the large 3D area.
Choose File > Save As. Open Documents. Use the New Folder button to create Atticus-AI-Builder, then open that folder. Name the file Hover-One-v01.blend. Click Save As and confirm if asked. Press Ctrl+S after each finished part.
CHECK: Your project is now in Documents > Atticus-AI-Builder. The starter stays unchanged.
Learn the few controls you need — 1:40-1:45 · Read this first
A model is a 3D object you can turn around. You will make seven parts: a body, a dark window cover, four engines and a rear wing. The picture shows the body and window cover. It is a real render of the lesson model, not a picture of Blender’s buttons.
Keep the mouse pointer over the large 3D picture before using a shortcut. The top-left menu should say Object Mode. Click a part to select it; an orange outline means that part is selected. Ctrl+Z undoes a mistake.
Shift+A opens the Add menu. Choose Mesh > Cube. A new cube starts at the centre. F2 lets you name it. Press Enter after typing its name.
Press N over the 3D picture. In the panel that opens on the right, select Item. Under Transform, Location means where the part sits; Dimensions means its size. X goes across, Y goes front to back, and Z goes up. Double-click a number, type its replacement, then press Enter. Copy the supplied settings; no calculations are needed.
After setting a part’s size, press Ctrl+A and choose Scale. This keeps its new shape while resetting its size controls. Press F3, type Add Bevel Modifier, and choose that result. A bevel trims sharp edges. Use its default 0.1 m amount and 1 segment. You can check them under the wrench icon on the right.
CHECK: Example: Dimensions X=3, Y=4.4, Z=0.6 makes a wide, low body. Location Z=1.1 lifts it above the stage.
Build the body and window cover — 1:45-1:55 · Your first two parts
Follow the controls you just learned. Finish one part before adding the next. The dark cover over the driver’s seat is called the canopy.
Add a cube and name it Body. In Item > Transform, set Dimensions to X 3, Y 4.4, Z 0.6. Set Location to X 0, Y 0, Z 1.1. Apply Scale and add the bevel, using the steps on the previous page.
Add a new cube and name it Canopy. Set Dimensions to X 1.8, Y 2.1, Z 0.65. Set Location to X 0, Y 0.15, Z 1.72. Apply Scale and add the bevel.
Look at the picture: the smaller cover sits on top of the larger body. Your shapes may still be grey. That is fine; paint comes after the engines. Press Ctrl+S.
CHECK: You have two separate parts. Selecting Canopy should outline only the smaller part.
Add four engines and a wing — 1:55-2:10 · Build the car’s shape
The engines sit beside the body. Make the first engine once, then copy it. A copy is called a duplicate. Copying saves time and keeps matching parts the same size.
Add a cube. Name it Front left. Set Dimensions to X 0.65, Y 1.35, Z 0.55. Set Location to X -1.65, Y -1.4, Z 0.85. Apply Scale and add the bevel.
With that engine selected, press Shift+D, then immediately press Esc. This makes a copy without moving it yet. Press F2 and name it Front right. In the Item panel, change only Location X to 1.65.
Copy Front right with Shift+D, then Esc. Name the copy Back right. Change only Location Y to 1.4. Copy Back right in the same way; name it Back left and change only Location X to -1.65. Do not add another bevel to copies: they already have one.
Add a new cube. Name it Rear wing. Set Dimensions to X 3.8, Y 0.55, Z 0.18. Set Location to X 0, Y 1.7, Z 1.8. Apply Scale and add the bevel. Press Ctrl+S.
CHECK: Count seven named car parts in the list at the top right. The studio items are extra; leave those alone.
Paint it, then ask AI for useful help — 2:10-2:20 · Give it a finished look
A material is the paint and surface finish of a part. The starter includes ready-made blue paint, dark glass and gold trim. You will assign them to your own shapes.
Select Body. In the tall Properties panel on the right, click Material Properties: the red sphere icon near the bottom. Below the empty material-slot box, click the small material sphere/dropdown beside New. Choose 01 Racing blue. Do not press New.
Repeat for Canopy, choosing 02 Dark canopy. Select each of the four engines and Rear wing in turn, choosing 03 Gold trim for each. If the colours are hidden, press Z over the 3D area and choose Material Preview from the pie menu. Wait for it to load.
Return to Virgil in the browser. Say: “I am making Hover One in Blender 5.2. My goal is a clear game-poster image. My car has a blue body, a dark canopy and four gold engines. Give me one small visual improvement I can make in five minutes. Tell me the exact Blender control. Keep the same project and software.”
If a suggestion is unclear, say: “Explain that in ordinary words and give me only the first click.” You can describe your screen or share a screenshot through an available upload control. Virgil cannot see Blender automatically. Make one change you understand, then check the car again. If it looks worse, use Ctrl+Z.
CHECK: A useful AI request says what you are making, what you see, what you want changed, and the help you need. Keep one suggestion that actually improves the picture.
Make the poster and keep your work — 2:20-2:30 · Render, save and reopen
Render means “make the finished picture using the camera and lights.” The .blend file keeps the editable car. The .png file is the picture you can show. You need both.
Press Ctrl+S. Check that your parent has set Render Properties > Render Engine to Cycles and Device to CPU. From the top menu choose Render > Render Image. Wait for the picture. Use this menu instead of F12 if your laptop intercepts function keys.
In the finished Render Result window, choose Image > Save As. Open Documents > Atticus-AI-Builder. Set the name to Hover-One-poster.png and File Format to PNG. Click Save As Image. Saving the Blender file alone does not save this picture.
Close the render window using its X to return to the model. Choose File > Save As and save a second version named Hover-One-v02.blend in the same folder. Keep v01 as your earlier copy.
Choose File > Open, select Hover-One-v02.blend and open it. Check that the seven parts and their colours are still there. Then use Windows File Explorer to open Hover-One-poster.png. Ask a parent to copy the whole Atticus-AI-Builder folder into the family’s existing backup location.
CHECK: You can reopen the editable car and its finished picture. GitHub is not needed today; no new account or public upload is part of this lesson.
Show what you made — 2:30-2:35 · Show, explain and stop
Now the teaching and building are complete. Show your work on the screen; you do not need to write a page of answers.
Show the saved poster. Point to the body, canopy, four engines and wing. Explain one thing you learned to do in Blender.
Show the change you tried after asking Virgil. Say what looked better, or why you undid it. AI’s idea is a suggestion; your picture is the test.
Open your saved .blend file and select one engine. This shows that you saved a model you can keep editing, not just a picture.
Next session: group the car’s parts and animate a short hover-and-turn shot. After that: add engine light, sound and a title to make a short reveal trailer. Keep today’s files. Do not start a new project.

worked_examples.title: One shape becomes a body
worked_examples.problem: A cube is too tall for a car body.
worked_examples.solution: In Item > Transform, set Dimensions X 3, Y 4.4, Z 0.6 and Location X 0, Y 0, Z 1.1. Apply Scale, then add a bevel.
worked_examples.explanation: Dimensions change its size. Location changes where it sits. The bevel trims the edges.

worked_examples.title: An AI request that can be answered
worked_examples.problem: “Make it better” does not tell Virgil what help you need.
worked_examples.solution: “I am on the engine-copy step in Blender 5.2. I pressed Shift+D then Esc. I see only one engine. Tell me the next click.”
worked_examples.explanation: The copy is on top of the first engine. Changing the copy’s Location separates them. A clear request names the tool, action and visible result.

Save this prepared starter with Ctrl+S. Use these settings for today’s small poster; the supplied file initially opens with Eevee. lessons.subject: literature
lessons.previous_learning: Friday: 90%. Read pages 81-93 for 25 minutes. Locator and alternative improved; keep/change needs a specific evidence link.
lessons.course_context: Day 29 builds from reviewed Day 28 work. Explain first; demonstrate; practice; check. Preserve original grades.
learning_objectives: Read for 25 minutes from the actual bookmark after page 93.
Connect one exact detail to a clearly stated idea.
lessons.why_it_matters: Read for 25 minutes from the actual bookmark after page 93.

vocabulary.definition: Something the book actually says happened.
An idea about what might explain the mystery.
Another possible explanation.

lessons.written_instruction:
TIME CAP: 35 minutes. 2:45-3:20. Stop at the end of this block.
2:45-3:10 READ. Open The Westing Game at your actual bookmark after page 93. If the bookmark differs, record the real page. Read for 25 minutes; do not rush toward a fixed ending page.
3:10-3:17 RECORD ONE CLUE. Name an exact action or words and where you found them. Say clearly what you think happened. A theory is an idea you are trying to check. Give another possible meaning. Then explain keep or change using that exact detail, not just I need more evidence.
Useful frame: I will keep/change the idea that ___ because on page/chapter ___, ___. This makes my idea more/less likely because ___. A clue can fit more than one person. It does not automatically prove who caused an event.
3:17-3:20 EXIT. Point to the part of the book. Explain what the detail does NOT prove. No spoilers and no invented book events.

worked_examples.title: Keep, with a link
worked_examples.problem: Invented mystery: Mina’s umbrella is wet on page 6. Your theory is that she walked in the rain.
worked_examples.solution: I keep that idea as possible because the wet umbrella fits rain. But someone else may have used it.
worked_examples.explanation: The decision names the theory and connects a detail; it does not claim proof.

worked_examples.title: Change, with a link
worked_examples.problem: On page 8 of the invented story, Mina says she borrowed the wet umbrella after entering the house.
worked_examples.solution: I weaken my rain-walk idea because the umbrella could have become wet before Mina used it.
worked_examples.explanation: New information changes how strong the earlier clue is.

independent_practice.prompt: L1. Record actual starting page, ending page, and minutes read.
L2. Complete one clue card: exact detail; page/chapter; your idea; another possible meaning; keep/change with a clear reason using the book.
independent_practice.answer: Verify passage in student edition. Do not assume event/locator accuracy without the book.

exit_ticket.prompt: LE1. Point to your detail. Does it prove your theory, or only make it possible or more likely? Explain.
exit_ticket.answer: Distinguish evidence from proof, using actual passage.
